intro: Narita is known abroad for its airport and at home for the great temple of Naritasan, but on the quiet north side of the city, in Daikata, stands Makata Shrine and its wood of old cedars, a Chiba Prefecture natural monument. The biggest of them, the great cedar of Kōzu, is about 40 metres tall and said to be well over a thousand years old. A reader told us about it.
meta_description: The great cedar of Makata Shrine in Narita, Chiba: about 40 metres tall, said to be 1,200 to 1,400 years old, and how to find it.

trees.name: The Great Cedar of Makata Shrine

location.address: Makata Shrine (麻賀多神社), 1 Daikata, Narita, Chiba

trees.story:
The cedar behind Makata Shrine in Narita is said to be well over a thousand years old, and a reader who wrote to us about it puts it at 1,400. Japanese Wikipedia's account of the shrine gives the age handed down for the Kōzu no Ōsugi, the great cedar of Kōzu, as 1,200 to 1,300 years, and a Japanese travel guide calls it 1,400 and the biggest cedar in eastern Japan. None of them comes from a measured age that we have found, so read every one of those numbers as tradition.

What is measured is its size: about 40 metres tall and some eight to nine metres round the trunk, by both accounts. It stands in the shrine's own wood, more than twenty old cedars with evergreen oaks and chinquapins among them, and Chiba Prefecture has protected that wood as a natural monument since 1977. Makata Shrine sits in Daikata, on the quiet north side of Narita, a few kilometres from the airport that most visitors to the city never leave.

We do not have a photograph of the cedar yet that we may use. If you go, take one of the whole trunk from the ground and send it to us here, with your location, and it will lead this page.

Walk past the main hall and into the trees behind it; the great cedar is the one that makes the others look young.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the shrine wood behind the main hall: the cedar far thicker than the twenty-odd others around it, about eight metres round and some 40 metres tall.

Behind its main hall grows a wood of more than twenty old cedars, with evergreen oaks and chinquapins among them, which Chiba Prefecture has protected as a natural monument since 1977. The biggest tree in it is the Kōzu no Ōsugi, the great cedar of Kōzu: about 40 metres tall and some eight to nine metres round the trunk, by the accounts we have read. Its age is tradition rather than measurement. Japanese Wikipedia gives the age handed down as 1,200 to 1,300 years, a Japanese travel guide says 1,400 and calls it the largest cedar in eastern Japan, and a reader who told us about it also puts it at 1,400. We do not yet have a photograph of it that we may use. If you visit, a picture of the whole trunk with your location will lead the page.
